title: Example and non-example differ once
statement: Pair an example with a non-example that differs only in the defining feature, and say why the non-example fails by naming that feature, never an incidental property.
example: In one course, 53 of 58 vocabulary non-examples gave no reason why they were not examples.
detail: The reading course's static content audit found 53 of 58 vocabulary non-examples stating no reason they were not examples (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/course-red-team/SKILL.md`, line 396). A red-team addendum made the very different second example required, because the minimally different pair marks the boundary but only the very different example stops the over-generalisation the pair invites, and required a non-example's reason to name the defining method after one non-example made being big disqualifying (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/feedback-2026-08-06-addendum.md`, lines 150-170). A generic instruction BrainLift gives the variation rule behind it: vary surface features with the distinction held constant, or the distinction with surface features held constant, never both on one item. Choose the examples and non-examples so that only one rule fits. Add genuinely different examples and a boundary case that show where the concept stops applying.
against: The same BrainLift exempts wrong-rule comparisons from the one-difference rule, since their asymmetry is the point (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Generic Instruction BrainLift.md`, line 81). that every example and non-example states its reason is a convention; nothing checks it. The ledger is an unreviewed draft: every reviewer-comment cell in it is blank (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0147-draft-grade-3-science-ledger.qmd`).

draws the same line using only true statements, without ever voicing the misconception.
AlphaTok and the course's locked script skill use positive-only framing, so a contrastive true-fact pair COUNTS as the boundary.
A definition is ONE sentence, 20 words at the outside. An example is at most two sentences and 30 words; a non-example at most two and 35, the extra five being the "because" R-VOC-4 requires.
Every extra clause is another place the two sides differ, so a long pair is a weaker contrast, not a more thorough one. The child then has to find the difference instead of being unable to miss it.
A 52-word non-example, which is what the `epic` card carried, is past the point where a nine-year-old can still hold the example it is supposed to be compared against.
The wording principle itself is not machine checkable and stays a review question: read the pair aloud and hear whether the two sides say the same thing until the moment they differ.

The test each candidate has to pass is R-VOC-3, an Engelmann minimal pair where the example and the non-example are the same situation with one feature changed, and R-VOC-4, a because-clause on the non-example saying why it is not an instance.
